overviewSummary.sv: Before this change, `Link.connect` made one call to `transport.open` and returned the boolean it got. Now it tries up to `maxAttempts` times (default 3) and waits a little longer after each failed attempt. It returns an `Outcome` of `'connected'` or `'gave-up'`. It also tells a single registered callback the outcome, through `setTimeout(…, 0)`. `startSession` now takes a `report` function. It registers a callback that reports `'session ready'` or `'offline mode'`, and it also reports `'retrying later'` itself when the outcome is `'gave-up'`.

It also tells a single registered callback the outcome, through `setTimeout(…, 0)`. `startSession` now takes a `report` function. It registers a callback that reports `'session ready'` or `'offline mode'`, and it also reports `'retrying later'` itself when the outcome is `'gave-up'`.

overview.sv:
Before this change, `Link.connect` made one call to `transport.open` and returned the boolean it got. Now it tries up to `maxAttempts` times (default 3) and waits a little longer after each failed attempt. It returns an `Outcome` of `'connected'` or `'gave-up'`. It also tells a single registered callback the outcome, through `setTimeout(…, 0)`. `startSession` now takes a `report` function. It registers a callback that reports `'session ready'` or `'offline mode'`, and it also reports `'retrying later'` itself when the outcome is `'gave-up'`.

The outcome reaches the session in two ways. One is the awaited return value of `connect`, which resumes `startSession` in a microtask. The other is the `whenSettled` callback, which `settle` puts on a macrotask timer. So the two reports come in a fixed order that the code doesn't state anywhere: the callback runs only after `startSession` has resumed from `connect` and run to the end.

The callback is one-shot: `settle` clears it, and a later `whenSettled` call replaces any earlier one. `transport.open` is not wrapped in a try/catch, so a rejection skips `settle` completely.

`startSession` now has a third required parameter. These revisions contain no other callers or tests.

title.sv: Starting a session when the link connects
title.en: Starting a session when the link connects

purpose.sv: Shows how `startSession` registers its callback, how `connect` gets to `'connected'`, and why `'session ready'` is reported only after `startSession` has finished.
purpose.en: Shows how `startSession` registers its callback, how `connect` gets to `'connected'`, and why `'session ready'` is reported only after `startSession` has finished.

question.sv: What happens, and in what order, when a session starts and the transport opens?
question.en: What happens, and in what order, when a session starts and the transport opens?

summary.sv: The session hands Link a callback that turns the outcome into a report, then awaits connect.
summary.en: The session hands Link a callback that turns the outcome into a report, then awaits connect.

body.sv:
This is where a session begins. In the earlier revision, `startSession` only awaited `link.connect(address)` and reported nothing. Now it takes a third parameter, `report`, which is a function that accepts a piece of text. The session uses it to tell its caller how the connection turned out. `startSession` doesn't decide what happens to that text, whether it's logged or shown to a user. It only calls `report`. No caller of `startSession` exists in this code, so it can't be seen what any real caller passes as `report`.

**First line: a callback is registered.** The argument given to `link.whenSettled` is an arrow function. In TypeScript, `(outcome) => ...` creates a function value without running it. `startSession` hands this function to the `Link` so that the `Link` can call it later, once the connection attempt has *settled*, meaning it has a final outcome. This is what "callback" means here. The function's body maps the outcome to a message:

- `'connected'` becomes `'session ready'`
- anything else becomes `'offline mode'`

`Outcome` is declared in `link.ts` as `'connected' | 'gave-up'`, so "anything else" can only be `'gave-up'`.

**Registering doesn't report anything.** When this line finishes, `report` hasn't been called. The `Link` has only stored the function. The next step shows how `whenSettled` keeps it.

**Second line: `connect` is awaited.** Because `startSession` is an `async` function, `await link.connect(address)` suspends `startSession` until the promise from `connect` resolves. Then the function continues with the result in `outcome`. The walk follows that call into `connect` in a later step.

This means the session has two separate ways to report:

1. the registered callback, which the `Link` decides when to call
2. the direct `report('retrying later')` that comes after the await

To judge this change you need to know in what order these two paths run. This walk and the next one work that out.

summary.sv: Link keeps a single nullable callback field, and each call overwrites it.
summary.en: Link keeps a single nullable callback field, and each call overwrites it.

body.sv:
The `whenSettled` call from the previous step (W1.1) lands here. In the earlier revision, `Link` had no state of its own: it held a `transport` and passed `connect` straight through to it. With this change, a `Link` object now remembers two things between calls.

**`onSettled` is a single slot for one callback.** Its type, `((outcome: Outcome) => void) | null`, means the field holds either a function that takes an `Outcome`, or `null` when nothing is registered. It starts as `null`. `whenSettled` assigns the given callback to this field and does nothing else. It doesn't call the callback, check what's already there, or queue anything.

Because there is only one slot, **a second `whenSettled` call replaces the first callback, and nothing tells the first registrant that its callback was dropped**. For example, if two pieces of code shared one `Link` and each called `startSession`, only the callback registered last would be stored. Whether callers ever share a `Link` like this can't be seen in this code, because nothing in the repository calls `startSession`. The only places that read or clear `onSettled` are `settle` and this assignment. Step W1.4 shows `settle` taking the callback out of the slot.

**`attempts` and `maxAttempts` hold the retry state.** `attempts` is a counter stored on the object and starts at 0. `maxAttempts` is a constructor parameter that defaults to 3. In TypeScript, writing `private readonly` before a constructor parameter makes that parameter a field automatically. So `new Link(transport)` gives a limit of 3, and `new Link(transport, 5)` gives 5. Existing code that calls `new Link(transport)` still compiles. In the next step (W1.3), `connect` resets `attempts` and counts it up to `maxAttempts`.

details.sv: `attempts` lives on the `Link` object rather than as a local variable inside `connect`. As a result, every `connect` call on the same `Link` shares one counter. The next step shows `connect` setting it back to 0 at the start of each call. Nothing in `connect` prevents two calls from overlapping on the same `Link`. title.sv: connect tries the transport in a loop
title.en: connect tries the transport in a loop

summary.sv: connect resets the attempt count, then awaits transport.open on each pass of the loop.
summary.en: connect resets the attempt count, then awaits transport.open on each pass of the loop.

body.sv:
This is the code that runs when `startSession` (W1.1) executes `await link.connect(address)`. In the earlier revision, `connect` was a single line, `return this.transport.open(address)`. It made one attempt and passed back the transport's `boolean` unchanged. Now `connect` retries, and it returns an `Outcome`, either `'connected'` or `'gave-up'`, instead of a `boolean`. Because the return type changed, any other caller that used the old `true`/`false` result would have to change too. In this code, `startSession` is the only caller.

What happens on each call:

1. **Reset.** `attempts` is set to 0. As described in W1.2, the counter belongs to the `Link` object, so every `connect` call starts counting again from zero.
2. **Loop bound.** The `while` loop runs as long as `attempts < maxAttempts`. `attempts` is increased at the start of each pass, so with the default `maxAttempts` of 3 the transport is tried at most three times.
3. **Awaited open.** `transport.open(address)` returns a `Promise<boolean>`. The `await` pauses `connect` until that promise resolves, and `open` then holds the result. While `connect` is paused, nothing in this function runs. JavaScript can do other work in the meantime, and `startSession` stays suspended at its own `await`.

**In this walk, `open` is `true`.** `connect` calls `this.settle('connected')` and then returns `'connected'`. The order matters. `settle` runs completely before the `return`. Returning from an `async` function is what resolves the promise `startSession` is waiting on. The next step (W1.4) shows that `settle` doesn't call the registered callback at this point. It only schedules it.

When `open` is `false`, the code takes the other path: it pauses and tries again. Walk W2 comes back to this point to follow that case.

title.sv: settle defers the callback to a timer
title.en: settle defers the callback to a timer

summary.sv: settle clears the stored callback and schedules it with setTimeout(…, 0).
summary.en: settle clears the stored callback and schedules it with setTimeout(…, 0).

body.sv:
`connect` calls this method on its success branch, just before it returns `'connected'` (W1.3). `settle` is a normal synchronous method. It finishes before `connect` moves on to its `return`. It does two things:

1. **It empties the slot first.** It copies the stored callback into the local variable `callback` and then sets `onSettled` to `null`. Each registered callback can therefore be scheduled at most once. A later `settle`, for example from another `connect` call, finds `null` and does nothing, unless `whenSettled` has registered a new callback in the meantime (W1.2). If nothing was registered at all, `settle` schedules nothing.
2. **It schedules the callback instead of calling it.** `setTimeout(() => callback(outcome), 0)` puts a timer task on JavaScript's event loop, and `settle` returns straight away. The callback hasn't run when `settle` returns.

The delay of `0` doesn't mean "now". The JavaScript runtime finishes the code it is currently running, plus all **microtasks** queued during that run, before it starts any timer task. A microtask is short follow-up work queued by promises. The continuation after an `await` is one. The language and the event-loop rules guarantee this order. It doesn't depend on how fast the machine is.

What follows for this walk: after `settle` returns, `connect` returns `'connected'`. That resolves the promise `startSession` is awaiting, so the continuation of `startSession` is queued as a microtask. **That microtask runs before the timer that `settle` just created**. So `startSession` resumes and finishes (W1.5) before the callback reports `'session ready'` (W1.6).

details.sv:
The arrow function given to `setTimeout` is a closure. It captures the local `callback` and `outcome`, not the field `onSettled`. A `whenSettled` call made after `settle` but before the timer fires therefore doesn't change or cancel the callback already queued. It only fills the now-empty slot for a later `settle`. Nothing in `Link` keeps the timer's handle, so a queued callback can't be cancelled.

The same ordering also covers code that awaits `startSession`. Those continuations are microtasks too, so they run before the timer as long as they only wait on promises that are already resolved. If such a caller awaits something that needs a new timer or I/O, the code allows the callback to run first. That depends on the caller, and no caller exists in this code.

summary.sv: With 'connected', startSession reports nothing itself and resolves.
summary.en: With 'connected', startSession reports nothing itself and resolves.

body.sv:
Execution is back in `startSession`, at the `await link.connect(address)` it was paused on (W1.1). `connect` returned `'connected'`, so `outcome` is `'connected'`. As W1.4 explained, this continuation runs as a microtask, before the timer that `settle` queued.

The check `outcome === 'gave-up'` is false, so `startSession` skips `report('retrying later')` and reaches its end. When an `async` function reaches its end, the promise it returned resolves with `undefined`, which is what its `Promise<void>` type says.

**At this point `report` hasn't been called once.** A caller that runs `await startSession(...)` continues now. It knows the session started, but `'session ready'` hasn't been reported yet. That report is still waiting in the timer `settle` queued.

The next step leaves this call chain and follows that timer task.

title.sv: The timer runs the registered callback
title.en: The timer runs the registered callback

summary.sv: Later, on the timer task, the callback reports 'session ready'.
summary.en: Later, on the timer task, the callback reports 'session ready'.

body.sv:
This is the arrow function `startSession` registered in W1.1, now running. It isn't called from the previous step. The JavaScript event loop calls it: it starts the timer task that `settle` queued (W1.4), and that task runs `callback(outcome)` with `outcome` set to `'connected'`.

The function itself is unchanged since W1.1. The ternary maps `'connected'` to `'session ready'` and passes that text to `report`. This works even though `startSession` has already returned. The arrow function is a closure: it keeps a reference to the `report` parameter it was created with, so `report` is still usable after the function that received it has finished.

That gives the full order on the success path:

1. `startSession` registers the callback and awaits `connect`.
2. `connect` gets `true` from `transport.open`, and `settle` queues the callback on a timer.
3. `startSession` resumes, reports nothing, and resolves (W1.5).
4. On the timer task, the callback reports `'session ready'`.

**So `'session ready'` always comes after `startSession` has resolved, never as part of it.** This order follows from the event-loop rules described in W1.4. It comes from reading the code. No test run was observed.

summary.en: When open is false, connect pauses attempts × 100 ms and loops again.

body.sv:
This walk starts again at the branch inside `connect`'s loop that W1.3 introduced. This time `transport.open` resolves to `false`. The `if (open)` block is skipped, so there is no `settle` and no `return`. Execution reaches `await pause(this.attempts * 100)` instead.

`attempts` was already increased at the start of this pass, so the wait grows with each failure. With the default `maxAttempts` of 3:

| Pass | `attempts` during the pass | `open` | Wait after it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | `false` | 100 ms |
| 2 | 2 | `false` | 200 ms |
| 3 | 3 | `false` | 300 ms |

After each wait the loop checks `attempts < maxAttempts` again. After the third pass, `3 < 3` is false and the loop ends. **The pause also runs after the last failed attempt**: `connect` waits 300 ms although no further attempt follows. With the defaults, that makes 600 ms of waiting before `connect` gives up. Whether that last wait is intended can't be read from the code. It is simply what the loop does.

`pause` is a small helper that turns a timer into a promise, so `connect` can `await` the delay the same way it awaits `transport.open`. While `connect` waits, it is suspended, and `startSession` is still paused at its own `await`. The next step shows `pause` itself.

details.sv: The wait grows linearly: it adds 100 ms per attempt. It doesn't double each time, which is what an exponential backoff would do. A larger `maxAttempts` passed to the constructor makes the waits longer as well. For example, with `maxAttempts` of 5 the waits are 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 ms, so 1.5 s in total.

title.sv: pause wraps setTimeout in a promise
title.en: pause wraps setTimeout in a promise

summary.sv: The helper resolves after the given number of milliseconds.
summary.en: The helper resolves after the given number of milliseconds.

body.sv:
`connect` reaches this helper from its `await pause(this.attempts * 100)` (W2.1). `new Promise(...)` takes a function, called the executor, and runs it immediately. The executor receives `resolve`, a function that fulfils the promise when it is called. Here the executor only starts a timer and gives `resolve` to it as the timer callback. So the promise from `pause` stays pending until the timer fires, and then it resolves with no value.

What this means for `connect`:

- **The wait is at least `ms` milliseconds.** The timer can't fire before then, and it can fire later if the event loop is busy.
- **The promise never rejects.** Only `resolve` is used, so `await pause(...)` can't throw.
- **The wait can't be cancelled.** The timer handle isn't kept, and `connect` takes no cancellation signal. Once `connect` starts waiting, it finishes the wait.

`pause` is declared at module level and isn't exported, so code outside `link.ts` can't call it. When the promise resolves, `connect` continues its loop and checks `attempts < maxAttempts` again. After the last attempt, the next step follows it out of the loop.

summary.sv: After the last attempt, connect settles with 'gave-up' and returns it.
summary.en: After the last attempt, connect settles with 'gave-up' and returns it.

body.sv:
`connect` gets here once `attempts < maxAttempts` is false. With the defaults, that is after the third failed attempt and its 300 ms pause (W2.1).

These two lines follow the same pattern as the success branch in W1.3, with `'gave-up'` in place of `'connected'`:

1. `settle('gave-up')` clears `onSettled` and queues the callback on a timer, as described in W1.4. The callback doesn't run yet. When it runs, it will receive `'gave-up'`.
2. `connect` returns `'gave-up'`. That resolves the promise `startSession` is awaiting, so `startSession` will resume in a microtask. **That microtask runs before the timer task just queued.** W1.4 explains why.

The next step follows `startSession` as it resumes with `'gave-up'`.

The next step follows `startSession` as it resumes with `'gave-up'`.

details.sv: The loop is the only way to reach this point without an error. If `maxAttempts` is 0 or less, the loop condition is false from the start, so `connect` never calls `transport.open`. It settles and returns `'gave-up'` straight away. The constructor accepts such a value without checking it. Whether any caller passes one can't be seen here: the only `Link` construction this code needs is `new Link(transport)` with the default of 3.

summary.sv: Resuming from the await, startSession reports 'retrying later' before the queued callback runs.
summary.en: Resuming from the await, startSession reports 'retrying later' before the queued callback runs.

body.sv:
This is the same place W1.5 showed, now reached with a different value. `connect` returned `'gave-up'` (W2.3), so `startSession` resumes from `await link.connect(address)` with `outcome` set to `'gave-up'`. As on the success path, this happens in a microtask, before any timer task (W1.4).

This time the check `outcome === 'gave-up'` is true, so `startSession` calls `report('retrying later')` directly, within the same microtask. Then it reaches its end, and its promise resolves.

The callback that `settle` queued is still waiting for its timer. It will report `'offline mode'` (next step). So **the caller's `report` receives `'retrying later'` first and `'offline mode'` second**. This order follows from the event-loop rules, not from timing. It is read from the code; no run was observed.

Read side by side, the two messages can look contradictory. One suggests the session will try again, the other that it has given up. Also, nothing in `startSession` or `Link` schedules another attempt after `'gave-up'`. Any retry would have to come from code outside this change. Whether that order and wording are intended is a question this code doesn't answer.

summary.sv: On the timer task, the registered callback maps 'gave-up' to 'offline mode'.
summary.en: On the timer task, the registered callback maps 'gave-up' to 'offline mode'.

body.sv:
This is the timer task that `settle('gave-up')` queued (W2.3). The JavaScript event loop starts it after `startSession` has already resolved (W2.4), and it calls the arrow function registered in W1.1 with `outcome` set to `'gave-up'`. As in W1.6, the closure still holds `report`.

This time the ternary's condition `outcome === 'connected'` is false, so the else arm is used and the callback reports `'offline mode'`. `Outcome` has only two values, so `'gave-up'` is the only value that reaches this arm.

That gives the full order on the path where every attempt fails, with the defaults:

1. Three calls to `transport.open` return `false`, with pauses of 100, 200 and 300 ms after them (W2.1).
2. `settle('gave-up')` queues the callback, and `connect` returns `'gave-up'` (W2.3).
3. `startSession` reports `'retrying later'` and resolves (W2.4).
4. On the timer task, the callback reports `'offline mode'`.

**The caller's `report` receives `'retrying later'` first and `'offline mode'` second, each exactly once.** This is read from the code; no test run was observed.

title.sv: A rejection leaves the loop without settling
title.en: A rejection leaves the loop without settling

summary.sv: The awaited open is not guarded, so a rejection propagates out of connect.
summary.en: The awaited open is not guarded, so a rejection propagates out of connect.

body.sv:
This walk goes back to the `await this.transport.open(address)` in `connect`'s loop, which W1.3 and W2.1 followed for `true` and `false`. There is a third possible outcome: `open` doesn't produce a `boolean` at all, because its promise **rejects** (fails with an error) or `open` throws.

When an `await` meets a rejected promise, it acts like a `throw` at that line, with the rejection's error. Code can catch that error only with a `try`/`catch` around the `await`, and `connect` has none. So execution leaves `connect` right there:

- Neither `settle('connected')` nor `settle('gave-up')` runs, so no callback is queued.
- `onSettled` keeps the callback registered by `startSession` (W1.2).
- `attempts` stays at the count it had reached. For example, if the first attempt returned `false` and the second rejected, `attempts` is 2, and the third attempt is never made.

An `async` function never throws to its caller directly. An error that escapes it rejects the promise the function returned. So **`connect` rejects with the transport's error** rather than returning an `Outcome`. The same happens if `open` throws synchronously instead of returning a rejected promise: inside an `async` function, that `throw` also becomes a rejection of `connect`'s promise.

The next step follows that rejected promise back to `startSession`.

details.sv: The leftover `attempts` value doesn't affect the next call, because `connect` sets it back to 0 at the start (W1.3). The leftover callback is different. Nothing clears it until a `settle` or a new `whenSettled` call. So a later `connect` on the same `Link` that does settle would call this old callback. The next step looks at what that means for `startSession`.

summary.sv: The await in startSession rethrows, so neither report is made.
summary.en: The await in startSession rethrows, so neither report is made.

body.sv:
`connect` rejected (W3.1), and the rejection arrives at `await link.connect(address)` in `startSession`. As in `connect`, an `await` on a rejected promise throws at that line. `startSession` has no `try`/`catch` either, so it stops there, and **the promise returned by `startSession` rejects with the transport's error**. Any caller that awaits `startSession` gets that error thrown at its own `await`.

Neither report is made:

- `report('retrying later')` comes after the `await`, so it never runs.
- The callback registered on the first line never runs, because no `settle` was reached and so nothing was queued (W1.4).

The caller learns about the failure only from the rejection, not through `report`. In the earlier revision, a rejection from `transport.open` also passed straight through `startSession`. What is new is that a rejection now gives no report, while the other two outcomes report through `report` twice or once.

**The callback stays registered on the `Link`.** It holds the `report` from this failed session. It is removed only when one of these happens:

- Another `whenSettled` call replaces it. A new `startSession` on the same `Link` does this as its first step, so a retry through `startSession` never runs the old callback.
- A later `connect` on the same `Link` reaches `settle`. That `settle` would queue this old callback. This can happen only if code calls `connect` without going through `startSession` first. Nothing in this code does, but nothing prevents it.
